notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 4:1–24, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Notes on Numbers 4:1–24

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron…"

**Traditional reading:** This verse opens the second census of the Levites. After the general numbering in chapter 3, God now commands a more specific census of those actually fit for active tabernacle service. The address to *both* Moses and Aaron underscores that priestly oversight is integral to the Levites' work.
- Keil & Delitzsch note the three families are now mustered for "the service to be performed by those who were between the ages of 30 and 50" — the *militia sacra* of Jehovah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)
- Gill: "After they had taken the number of the Levites, and made an exchange of the firstborn of Israel for them; and now they are ordered to number them a second time, and take out from them such as were fit for service." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 2 — "Take a census of the Kohathites among the Levites by their clans and families…"

**Traditional reading:** Kohath is dealt with first, even though Gershon was the eldest son of Levi (Num 3:17). The reason is the greater sanctity of the Kohathites' charge: they carry the most holy furnishings. God's ordering here is by holiness, not birth order.
- Ellicott: "Kohath appears to have been the second son of Levi, but the Kohathites here stand first because Moses and Aaron belonged to them, and it was their office to bear the Ark." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch: "The three families are not arranged according to the relative ages of their founders, but according to the importance or sacredness of their service." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word): "God elevates the unexpected. In the culture of the Old Testament, an elder son was always favored… It is not always so with God." He notes this pattern also seen in Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over Reuben, David over his brothers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill observes that some Jewish commentators thought Kohath came first because Moses and Aaron sprang from him, but Gill thinks "the true reason seems to be, because of the order observed in taking down the tabernacle… it was most proper and reasonable… first to take out the ark, table, &c. which was the business of the Kohathites." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "men from thirty to fifty years old—everyone who is qualified to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting."

**Traditional reading:** Thirty to fifty was considered the prime of life — a balance of physical strength and mature judgment. The Hebrew phrase translated "enter the host" (צָבָא, *tsava*) is military language; Levitical service is a sacred warfare.
- Ellicott: "The previous census of the Levites was from a month old. The present census was with a view to the discharge of duties requiring a considerable amount of physical strength… Thirty was the age at which John the Baptist and our Lord entered upon their public ministry." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Pulpit Commentary: "Thirty years became among the Jews the perfect age at which a man attained to full maturity" and notes the apparent discrepancy with Numbers 8:24 (age 25) — the LXX altered 30 to 25 to harmonise, but tradition reconciles the two by viewing 25–30 as a training period. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm)
- Gill, citing the Mishnah (Pirke Abot 5:21): "a son of thirty years for strength," adding that both John the Baptist and Christ began their ministry at thirty. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)
- Guzik: "The hint of 'warfare' in the phrase 'to perform the service' points to a deeper truth that serving the Lord… involves genuine spiritual conflict." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)

**Catholic (Haydock):** Notes the LXX reads "25" at v. 3; the traditional explanation is that they began learning at 25 but did not officiate until 30. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-4.html)

---

### v. 4 — "This service of the Kohathites at the Tent of Meeting regards the most holy things."

**Traditional reading:** "The most holy things" (*qodesh haqqodashim*) refers not only to the ark but to all the sacred furniture — the table of showbread, the lampstand, the altars, and their utensils. The phrase characterizes the dignity and gravity of the Kohathite charge.
- Precept Austin: "The most holy things…here the term is used for the furnishings in the sanctuary. In a sense the work of the Kohathites is what they are *not* to do with the holy things — touch or even see them!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary)
- Gill, citing Jarchi: the Kohathites' service included the showbread table, the candlestick, the altars, the veil, and ministering vessels — "more holy than all other things." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)
- Pulpit Commentary: "Rather, 'the most holy things:' they were the service of the Kohathites. So the Septuagint." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "Whenever the camp sets out, Aaron and his sons are to go in, take down the veil of the curtain, and cover the ark of the Testimony with it."

**Traditional reading:** The "covering veil" is the curtain that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place (Ex 26:31). Under normal circumstances, only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only on the Day of Atonement. But when the camp moved, the divine Presence departed in the cloud, permitting the priests to enter and pack.
- Ellicott: "Under ordinary circumstances the high priest himself might only enter the most holy place on one day in the year. At the time of the moving of the camp, however, the Divine Presence seems to have departed from the Holy of Holies, and to have ascended in the cloud which gave the signal for the removal." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Gill, citing Bishop Patrick: "the divine Majesty was gone from thence in the cloud which gave the signal for the motion of the camp." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)
- Guzik: "The ark of the covenant was holy, so it could only be covered and prepared for transport by the priests." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)

---

### v. 6 — "They are to place over this a covering of fine leather, spread a solid blue cloth over it, and insert its poles."

**Traditional reading:** The ark received three coverings: (1) the veil itself, (2) a covering of *tachash* skin (likely sea-cow or porpoise hide) for protection from weather, and (3) an outer cloth of solid blue, marking it as the throne of God. The blue outermost covering distinguished the ark from all other furnishings during the march. The staves (poles) were removed for wrapping and reinserted for carrying.
- Keil & Delitzsch: "The sea-cow skin was to protect the inner curtain… from storm and rain; the hyacinth purple, to distinguish the ark of the covenant as the throne of the glory of Jehovah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)
- Pulpit Commentary: "This was the distinctive outer, and therefore visible, covering of the most sacred thing, the ark." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/4.htm)
- Wenham (cited in Precept Austin): "Thus, when the camp was on the move, the ark was distinguished from all the other pieces of furniture by its blue outer cover." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary)
- Gill: notes debate over whether the blue cloth was outermost (for honour) or the badger skin was outermost (for protection). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 7 — "Over the table of the Presence they are to spread a blue cloth and place the plates and cups on it… The regular bread offering is to remain on it."

**Traditional reading:** The table of showbread was covered first with a blue cloth, then the vessels (dishes, pans, bowls, pitchers) were placed on top, and the showbread itself remained on the table even during transport. This indicates the bread was "continual" — present before the Lord even on the march.
- Ellicott: "The shew-bread is so called because it was renewed every Sabbath day, and was continually before the face of the Lord even (as it appears from this verse) during the marches of the Israelites through the desert." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Gill: "The shewbread is called 'continual', because it was always on the table… this bread seems at this time to be also placed upon the table, spread with the blue cloth; and from hence it appears, that the Israelites had the shewbread in the wilderness; for the making of which they might be supplied with corn from the neighbouring countries." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 8 — "And they shall spread a scarlet cloth over them, cover them with fine leather, and insert the poles."

**Traditional reading:** Over the vessels and bread, a scarlet (crimson) cloth was spread, then the protective leather covering, and finally the carrying poles inserted.
- Keil & Delitzsch: "a crimson cloth over these vessels and the shew-bread, and cover this with a sea-cow skin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)

---

### v. 9–10 — "They are to take a blue cloth and cover the lampstand used for light… wrap it and all its utensils inside a covering of fine leather and put it on the carrying frame."

**Traditional reading:** The lampstand (menorah) and all its accessories — lamps, wick-trimmers, trays, oil vessels — were wrapped first in a blue cloth, then in leather, and placed on a carrying frame (*mot*). Unlike the ark and table, the lampstand received only two coverings (no scarlet), reflecting its lesser sanctity.
- Gill: "the ark and the shewbread table had three coverings, but the candlestick only two, they being more sacred than that, especially the ark." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch identify the "carrying frame" (*mot*) as a bearing frame or bar. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)

---

### v. 11 — "Over the gold altar they are to spread a blue cloth, cover it with fine leather, and insert the poles."

**Traditional reading:** The golden altar (altar of incense, Ex 30:1) was treated similarly — blue cloth, leather, then poles. This altar stood in the Holy Place and was among the "most holy things."
- Gill: "The altar of incense, which was overlaid with gold, and therefore called a golden one, to which the allusion is in Revelation 8:3." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 12 — "They are to take all the utensils for serving in the sanctuary, place them in a blue cloth, cover them with fine leather, and put them on the carrying frame."

**Traditional reading:** This covers the miscellaneous vessels used by the priests in the Holy Place. Gill interprets "instruments of ministry" as possibly including the priestly garments: "The garments in which the priests ministered in the sanctuary, which were laid up in proper places, and which they only wore when in service." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 13–14 — "Then they shall remove the ashes from the bronze altar, spread a purple cloth over it, and place on it all the vessels… They are to spread over it a covering of fine leather and insert the poles."

**Traditional reading:** The bronze altar of burnt offering — located in the courtyard — was treated differently. It first had to be cleansed of ashes. It was covered with a *purple* cloth (not blue, marking its lesser sanctity as an outer-court item), then its implements (firepans, forks, shovels, basins) were placed on it, then a leather covering and poles. Purple distinguished it from the most holy items which were wrapped in blue.
- Wenham (Precept Austin): "The altar for burnt offering that stood in the court of the tabernacle was wrapped first in a purple cloth, and then in a goatskin cover." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary)
- Gill, citing Bishop Patrick: "the fire, which was always burning on it… was doubtless preserved, and care was taken for the carrying it along with the altar, or in a separate vessel from it." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

**Text-critical note (LXX/Samaritan):** Several commentaries note that the laver (bronze basin, Ex 30:18) is omitted from the Hebrew text here. The Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch supply an addition after v. 14 covering the laver. Keil & Delitzsch call this "a spurious interpolation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html) The Pulpit Commentary suggests the omission may have been accidental or the laver was carried uncovered. Guzik (Enduring Word) cites Cole: "The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint add the bronze laver… that is missing from the MT." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/) Gill suggests the laver may have been carried uncovered as a "lively representation of the grace of God in Christ, continuing and opened as an ever springing fountain." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 15 — "When Aaron and his sons have finished covering the holy objects… the Kohathites shall come and do the carrying. But they must not touch the holy objects, or they will die."

**Traditional reading:** This is the pivotal verse. The priests alone pack; the Kohathites carry — but only by the poles, never touching the holy things directly. The penalty for touching is death, as later illustrated by Uzzah (2 Sam 6:6–7).
- Ellicott: "The word which is rendered 'any holy thing' may here, as elsewhere, denote the sanctuary. This injunction is repeated in Numbers 18:3. We find in 2 Samuel 6:6-7 an instance of the fatal result of the violation of this command by Uzzah, who being, as is most probable, a Levite, and of the family of Kohath, ought to have been acquainted with the law." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch: "they were not to touch 'the holy' (the holy things), lest they should die." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)
- Guzik: "The Kohathites were forbidden to touch any of the tabernacle furniture. Only the priests could prepare the furnishings of the sanctuary; the sons of Kohath were commanded to carry them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)
- Precept Austin: "Service to Yahweh was serious business! And it still is beloved!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary)

---

### v. 16 — "Eleazar son of Aaron the priest shall oversee the oil for the light, the fragrant incense, the daily grain offering, and the anointing oil. He has oversight of the entire tabernacle…"

**Traditional reading:** Eleazar, as Aaron's eldest surviving son (after Nadab and Abihu's deaths), had personal charge of the four consumable holy items: oil, incense, grain offering, and anointing oil. He also had overall oversight. A comparison with vv. 28 and 33 shows Eleazar supervised the Kohathites while his younger brother Ithamar supervised the Gershonites and Merarites.
- Ellicott: enumerates each item — oil for the candlestick, incense of spices, the continual *minchah*, the anointing oil (Ex 30:23–31). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Constable (StudyLight): "The oils, incense, and the flour for the daily meal offering were the special responsibility of Eleazar, the heir to the high priest's office." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-4.html)
- Coffman: "It appears from a comparison of Numbers 4:16; Numbers 4:28 and Numbers 4:33 that the ministry of the Kohathites were superintended by Eleazar, and that of the Gershonites and the Merarites by Ithamar." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-4.html)

---

### v. 17–18 — "Do not allow the Kohathite tribal clans to be cut off from among the Levites."

**Traditional reading:** God urgently warns Moses and Aaron not to be negligent in following the packing procedures just described, because their carelessness could cause the death of the Kohathites. "Cut ye not off" means "take care that the Kohathites are not cut off through your mistake and negligence."
- Keil & Delitzsch: "In order to prevent as far as possible any calamity from befalling the Levites… the priests are again urged… 'cut ye not off,' i.e., 'take care that the Kohathites are not cut off through your mistake and negligence' (Ros.)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)
- Ellicott: "Moses and Aaron are charged not to be guilty of such negligence in respect of it as might expose the Kohathites to death… Moses and Aaron might be said to do that which would be the result of their negligence. In like manner St. Paul enjoins… 'Destroy not him with thy meat for whom Christ died' (Rom 14:15)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Gill: "give no occasion, as the Targum of Jonathan; or be not the cause of their cutting off, as Jarchi, through negligence or inadvertency of theirs, in packing up the above things." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

---

### v. 19 — "Aaron and his sons are to go in and assign each man his task and what he is to carry."

**Traditional reading:** Each Kohathite received a personal, individual assignment. Nothing was left to chance or personal preference; the priests appointed each man to a specific task under close supervision. This preserved order and prevented fatal mistakes.
- Guzik: "The Kohathites had a permanent place of service before the LORD… Even though their work was 'only' transporting the furnishings of the tabernacle, it was properly regarded as important, worthy service to God, deserving of a specific appointment." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)
- Precept Austin, citing Gilbrant: "The implication… is that the priests must protect the Kohathites from the danger of profanation of the holy things by closely supervising their work, lest the Kohathites be killed. The danger was real, as Korah was to discover." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-4-commentary)

---

### v. 20 — "But the Kohathites are not to go in and look at the holy objects, even for a moment, or they will die."

**Traditional reading:** The prohibition is double — they must not touch (v. 15) and must not even *look* at the uncovered holy things. The Hebrew expression translated "even for a moment" is literally "like a swallowing" (*ke-balla*), meaning an instant — as long as it takes to gulp something down. Mere curious gazing at the unveiled holy things would bring death.
- Keil & Delitzsch: "If the Kohathites should come for only a single moment to look at the holy things, they would die. כבלע, 'like a swallow, a gulp,' is probably a proverbial expression… for 'a single instant.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html)
- Ellicott: "But they shall not go in to see the holy things (or, the sanctuary) for a moment. The Levites were not permitted to enter the holy place in which the priests ministered, much less the Holy of Holies." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Coffman: "The words from which 'even for a moment' are rendered have the meaning of 'even as long as it takes to swallow.'" Orlinsky rendered it: "They shall not witness the dismantling of the sanctuary." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-4.html)
- Catholic (Haydock): "Septuagint, 'suddenly.' Let them not rush in before all the vessels be properly covered. The priests folded them up with all haste, that they might see them as little as possible themselves." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-4.html)
- Guzik: "The Kohathites were not to even look at the holy things as the priests covered them and prepared them for moving… The penalty for going beyond what God had appointed could be death." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)
- Gill sees a typological meaning: "which may signify the hiding of the mysteries of grace in those things under the former dispensation, when even the Levites themselves were not admitted to a sight of them; see Ephesians 3:4." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)

**Illustration:** Both Keil & Delitzsch and Ellicott note 1 Samuel 6:19 (the men of Beth-shemesh struck down for looking into the ark) as a historical illustration of this principle.

---

### v. 21–23 — Census of the Gershonites (30–50 years old)

**Traditional reading:** The Gershonites are now numbered. Although Gershon was Levi's firstborn, he is treated second because his family's charge (the curtains and coverings) was less sacred than the Kohathites' charge of the furniture. The age range and military language ("enter to perform the service" = "war the warfare") are identical to v. 3.
- Ellicott: simply notes the parallel structure. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Guzik notes the phrasing "to war the warfare" and its application: "when one begins to serve the LORD, His people, and a needy world in the name of Jesus, the warfare begins." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)
- Haydock (Catholic): repeats the note about the LXX reading 25, with Du Hamel: "They began to be taught how to act, at 25; but did not officiate till 30." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-4.html)

---

### v. 24 — "This is the service of the Gershonite clans regarding work and transport…"

**Traditional reading:** The Gershonites carried all the fabric components: the tabernacle curtains (fine linen), the tent curtains (goats' hair), the rams' skin covering, the outer leather covering, the screen for the entrance, the court hangings, the gate screen, cords, and all associated equipment. Their work was supervised by Ithamar (v. 28), not Eleazar.
- Gill, citing Aben Ezra: the phrase "to serve" refers to setting up the tabernacle, making the showbread, slaying sacrifices, and guarding; "for burdens" refers to carrying when journeying. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm)
- Ellicott: "The curtains of the *mishkan* are represented in Exodus 26:6 as constituting the *mishkan* itself, the woodwork being apparently regarded as subsidiary to the curtains." He distinguishes the fine linen curtains of the dwelling from the goats' hair curtains of the tent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm)
- Guzik: "While the Kohathites were responsible for carrying the furnishings of the tabernacle, the Gershonites were responsible for carrying the tabernacle coverings." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/)

---

## Summary of Denominationally Distinct Readings

Across the sources consulted, **there is remarkably little doctrinal disagreement** among Protestant traditions on this passage. The chapter is largely descriptive and procedural, so differences are minor:

| Tradition | Distinctive Emphasis | Source |
|-----------|---------------------|--------|
| **Reformed / Lutheran** (Keil & Delitzsch) | Emphasises precise lexical detail, the *militia sacra* concept, and the theologically graded holiness of the three families arranged by sanctity not birth. | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-4.html |
| **Anglican** (Ellicott) | Notes typological connections (30 years = age of Christ and John the Baptist), the exception to the high priest's entry rules, and parallels Paul's "destroy not" language in Romans 14:15. | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/4.htm |
| **Baptist / Reformed Baptist** (Gill) | Typical rabbinic engagement (Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Mishnah); suggests a Christological typology in the laver being uncovered (an ever-springing fountain of grace) and in the hidden holy things veiling the "mysteries of grace" until Christ (Eph 3:4). | https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/4.htm |
| **Pentecostal / Charismatic** (Guzik, Enduring Word) | Stresses practical application — God elevates the unexpected, every role matters, the "warfare" language applies to all Christian service, and behind-the-scenes work is sacred. | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-4/ |
| **Catholic** (Haydock) | Follows the LXX age of 25; notes that eventually priests carried the ark themselves (Deut 31:9) once numerous enough; emphasises priestly haste and restriction of curiosity. | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-4.html |

On matters of **textual criticism** (the missing laver, the age discrepancy with Num 8:24), the sources all note the same issues. Keil & Delitzsch defend the MT against LXX/Samaritan additions. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott acknowledge the LXX variant without dogmatism.

No distinctively **Prosperity, Word of Faith, or Hyper-Grace** readings were found in the accessible sources for this passage.
